# Stereogram

> A free stereogram (Magic Eye) generator that runs entirely in the browser. Pick a shape, type a
> word, paint a relief or upload a depth map; choose random dots or a pattern; download a PNG at
> screen, phone-wallpaper or A4 print size. English interface. No account, no ads, nothing is
> uploaded, and the page works offline once loaded.

## What it is
- Single-image stereograms (autostereograms) after Thimbleby, Inglis & Witten (IEEE Computer, 1994), with hidden-surface removal, parallel or cross-eyed viewing, adjustable eye separation and depth of field.
- Depth sources: 26 real sculptures (CC0, Poly Haven) baked to depth maps, eight built-in shapes, hidden text, a soft-brush drawing, or any greyscale picture (white = near).
- Patterns: 36 ornament tiles from The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection (CC0: katagami stencils, Iznik tiles, Coptic textiles, wallpapers), black-and-white random dots with adjustable density, colour dots, three procedural tiles, or a picture of your own. Every picture prints the provenance of its figure and pattern.
- Reproducible: a seed and a shareable link recreate the same picture pixel for pixel.
- Open source, MIT.

## How to use it
- https://stereogram.dravec.org/ — make one; the first picture appears without any input.
- https://stereogram.dravec.org/?text=HELLO — a link with parameters opens that exact picture (shape, text, seed, size, pattern, depth, mode).
- https://stereogram.dravec.org/#/book/1 — a book of 100 plates, one per screen, with the answer one tap away and a link to make your own from any plate.
- https://stereogram.dravec.org/#/see — how to see a stereogram, a six-step practice ladder, and the honest note that about one adult in fourteen cannot.

## Data & provenance
- Figures: Poly Haven models (CC0), baked at build time by scripts/bake-library.mjs. Patterns: The Met Open Access API, isPublicDomain items only (CC0). The provenance of every asset is in src/library/provenance.json and printed under each picture. Rendering is deterministic code in the page; nothing leaves the browser except anonymous first-party usage counts (no cookies).
